opus-5.5.text:
I think both are important, and they're complementary rather than competing. Cross-lingual transfer has been surprisingly effective in practice. When you train a large multilingual model, a lot of what it learns about one language does seem to carry over to others, especially for languages that are typologically similar or share a script, and that's given us real gains for languages that don't have billions of words of text on the web. So from an engineering standpoint, that's probably the approach that will pay off soonest.

But I'd be cautious about treating transfer as the whole solution. For one thing, it works much better for some languages than others. If your language is structurally very different from the high-resource languages that dominate the training data, say it has very rich morphology or a different word order, the model may end up imposing English-like or European-like generalizations on it. There's also the "curse of multilinguality": as you add more languages, you're dividing a fixed capacity among them, and the low-resource languages tend to get the short end of that.

That's part of why I'm personally excited about data-efficient learning, and it connects to my broader research interests. Children acquire language from something like tens of millions of words, orders of magnitude less than what our models see. That gap tells us there are inductive biases, ways of generalizing, that we haven't figured out how to build into our systems. If we could close even part of that gap, the benefits would go beyond low-resource languages. We'd have models that generalize in more human-like ways, that are more robust out of distribution, and that are cheaper to train.

So my view is that transfer is the pragmatic near-term path, and data efficiency is the more fundamental scientific question. Ideally they'll meet in the middle: better inductive biases will make transfer work better too, because the model will learn more abstract, genuinely linguistic representations rather than surface patterns tied to a particular language.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts children’s data exposure with models’ much larger training sets, but does not say that this gap is increasing.

r002.rationale: It says low-resource languages lack billions of words of web text, identifying limited text availability as a constraint.

r003.rationale: It describes transfer as effective but uneven and limited; it does not frame how much English-learned knowledge transfers as an open question.

r004.rationale: It presents cross-lingual transfer as a pragmatic path that benefits low-resource languages alongside data-efficient learning, and says improving inductive biases could make transfer work better.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think of those two as complementary rather than competing, but I'm honestly more excited, scientifically, about data efficiency, because that's where the gap between humans and current models is most glaring.

Here's the framing I keep coming back to. A child learning Hebrew or Basque or any language gets on the order of tens of millions of words by the time they're a fluent speaker. The models we train on English see thousands of times that. So when we say a language is "low-resource," we're really saying it's low-resource relative to an absurd standard that our architectures have set. The language isn't the problem; our inductive biases are. If we understood what makes human learners so efficient, the low-resource problem would mostly dissolve, because almost every language on earth has more text than a child ever hears.

Cross-lingual transfer, by contrast, is the pragmatic solution we have right now, and it works reasonably well, but I think we should be clear-eyed about what it's doing. A lot of the transfer we see is piggybacking on shared vocabulary, shared scripts, typological similarity, or parallel content like Wikipedia that exists across languages. When you look at languages that are genuinely distant from the high-resource ones, especially morphologically rich languages, or languages with very different word order, performance drops off quite steeply. And there's also a cultural dimension that gets flattened: you end up with a model that speaks the language but thinks like an English Wikipedia article.

What I'd love to see is for these two threads to actually meet. The multilingual setting is a wonderful natural experiment for studying inductive biases. If we can measure how much data a model needs to acquire, say, agreement or case marking in language X given pretraining on language Y, that tells us something about what abstractions the model has formed. Is it learning something like a grammatical category of subject, or just surface statistics that happen to overlap? Work like the BabyLM efforts, where we constrain the training budget to something human-scale, is pushing in that direction, and I think multilingual variants of that are exactly the right next step.

So my short answer is: transfer is the near-term win and we should keep improving it, but if the field invests only there, we'll keep patching symptoms. The deeper and more generalizable payoff is in figuring out how to learn from less, and the languages with less data are precisely where that research is both most needed and most informative.

r001.rationale: The response says the model–human data gap is glaring and gives its scale, but does not say that the gap is increasing.

r002.rationale: It contrasts English-scale model training with what humans hear, but does not identify limited text availability in smaller languages as a constraint on matching English-scale datasets.

r003.rationale: It describes weaker performance for distant languages and proposes studying transfer, but does not frame how much English-learned knowledge transfers to low-resource languages as an open question.

r004.rationale: It presents data efficiency and cross-lingual transfer as complementary approaches, describing transfer as the pragmatic near-term way to improve low-resource language performance.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re complementary, but they address somewhat different questions. With cross-lingual transfer, you’re asking whether the resources we have for a language like English can help us build a system for a language where we have much less data. That’s a very useful practical approach. But its success will depend on what the languages share, and we shouldn’t assume that everything we learn from English will transfer equally well.

Data-efficient learning asks a more fundamental question: why does the system need so much data in the first place? Humans can learn a language without first learning English or having access to enormous amounts of text. That suggests there’s room to improve the learning process itself, although children also have access to interaction and other kinds of information that a text-only model doesn’t.

So I’d want to pursue both. Transfer can help us make better use of the resources we already have, while data efficiency could make us less dependent on having a well-resourced language to transfer from. And we need to evaluate those approaches across languages with different properties, rather than treating performance on English as evidence that we’ve solved language learning generally.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts humans’ ability to learn without enormous text datasets with models’ data needs, but does not say that the gap between their training-data amounts is increasing.

r002.rationale: It says some languages have much less data than English, but does not identify text availability in smaller languages as a constraint on matching English-scale training datasets.

r003.rationale: It says transfer depends on what languages share and cautions that English-derived learning may not transfer equally, presenting the extent of transfer as uncertain.

r004.rationale: It presents cross-lingual transfer and data-efficient learning as complementary routes: transfer uses existing resources, while data efficiency reduces dependence on a well-resourced language.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re complementary. With cross-lingual transfer, you can take advantage of what a model has learned from languages with a lot of available text. That’s a promising way to improve performance on a language where you have much less data. But it doesn’t eliminate the question of data efficiency; it shifts some of the learning to other languages.

If we’re interested in how children learn language, that distinction matters. A child isn’t coming to their first language having already read billions of words in a hundred other languages. So transfer might be very useful from an engineering perspective without giving us an explanation of human learning.

And for languages with less training data, I wouldn’t assume that transfer will give us everything we need. There may be properties of those languages that aren’t well represented in the languages the model was trained on. We still want models that can learn something new from a small amount of evidence. So I’d pursue both, while being clear about what question each approach is answering.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that the gap between model and human training data is increasing.

r002.rationale: It mentions languages with much less data, but does not identify text availability as a constraint on matching English-scale datasets.

r003.rationale: It raises limits to transfer from languages with abundant text, but does not specifically discuss transfer from large amounts of English data.

r004.rationale: It presents cross-lingual transfer as a promising way to improve low-resource performance and says to pursue it alongside data efficiency.
